scenario: Today's generative track has a single paper, and it asks whether a long history can be compressed into a fixed-size memory without dropping the signals needed for prediction. Once a generative recommender feeds very long interactions straight into the model, compute and memory grow with length. This paper writes history into a fixed number of memory slots segment by segment, and uses a fixed-length context at decode time. On a long-sequence e-commerce benchmark, the compressed model still approaches a counterpart that processes the long history directly, and distant behavior still contributes signal. For teams that want to serve long-sequence generative recommenders, the point is not to stretch the attention window without limit, but to keep the memory stable and usable as the history keeps growing.

papers.title: RecMem: Recurrent Memory Compression for Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Haoyi Hu, Gaoyang Guo, Yunjia Xi, Wen Chen, Weiwen Liu, Jian Wu, Yuning Jiang, Weinan Zhang
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.

papers.summary: Once a generative recommender feeds a user's long history straight into the model, compute and memory grow with history length, and long interaction sequences quickly become slow and expensive. The authors compress history segment by segment into a fixed number of memory slots, and the decoder uses a fixed-length context that no longer expands as the history grows. On a long-sequence benchmark from an e-commerce platform, decoder context falls from 1,200 tokens to 216, while the model still retains 87.9% of the Recall@10 of a counterpart that processes the same-length history directly, and recall at deeper cutoffs stays nearly comparable. The same trained model does not collapse in recommendation quality over a much longer stream of later interactions. ==Signals in distant behavior can be kept without feeding the entire history into the decoder==. For teams that want to serve long-sequence generative recommenders, this is a way to trade a fixed-size memory for context, instead of keeping the whole history in the attention window.
